summary: Specifies the message protocol Sun Microsystems and others used for Remote Procedure Call (RPC), proposed for the Internet's consideration. It was not an Internet standard. It is now historic, and was replaced by RFC 1057.

eli5.summary: Normally a program calls a function inside itself. Remote procedure call lets it call one in another computer as though it were close by.

questions: how does remote procedure call work
what is the rpc message protocol
subtitle: The message protocol for calling functions in remote computers

tldr.problem: Programs need a standard way to call functions in other computers across a network, as if they were local function calls.
tldr.mechanism: Sun's RPC protocol packages a procedure call as a message sent to a server, which executes the procedure and sends back a message with the result. The protocol includes support for different transport methods, authentication, program versioning, and error handling.
tldr.outcome: This protocol was not adopted as an Internet standard but was widely used by Sun and others. It was replaced by RFC 1057, which was the official standard version of the same protocol.

today: RFC 1050 is Historic. It was the original specification for Sun Microsystems' Remote Procedure Call protocol but was superseded by RFC 1057, which is the official Internet standard version with minor corrections and clarifications. Most modern systems now use a later version of RPC or alternative distributed computing frameworks.

sections.title: Introduction and Model
sections.content:
RFC 1050 specifies the message protocol that Sun Microsystems uses to implement Remote Procedure Call (RPC). RPC allows a program on one computer to call a function on another computer, and the protocol is transport-independent, meaning it works over TCP/IP, UDP/IP, or other network protocols.

The RPC model is based on the familiar local procedure call. When a program calls a local function, it places arguments in a well-known location, transfers control to the function, and waits for the result. Remote procedure call works similarly: the client sends a message containing the procedure parameters to the server, blocks waiting for a reply, and then extracts the results when the reply arrives. On the server side, a process waits for incoming call messages, extracts the parameters, computes the result, and sends a reply message.

The protocol defines three levels of identification for a procedure: the program number (which remote program), the program version (which version of that program), and the procedure number (which function within the program). Program numbers below 0x20000000 are administered by Sun, while numbers from 0x20000000 to 0x3fffffff are reserved for user-defined programs. This allows multiple versions of a program to coexist on the same server for backward compatibility.
sections.eli5: RPC lets one computer ask another computer to run a program and send back the answer. The message says which program, which version of it, and which function to run.

sections.title: Transports and Message Semantics
sections.content:
RPC is independent of the underlying transport protocol. If RPC runs on a reliable transport like TCP/IP, the application can infer that a procedure was executed exactly once when a reply is received, and if no reply arrives after a crash or network failure, it cannot assume the procedure was not executed. If RPC runs on an unreliable transport like UDP/IP, it provides no reliability guarantees, and the application must implement its own retransmission and timeout policies.

The RPC protocol itself does not provide any reliability, duplication detection, or ordering guarantees. The protocol includes a transaction ID (xid) in every message, which the client uses to match replies to requests. A server may use this ID to implement execute-at-most-once semantics: by remembering the ID after granting a request, the server can refuse to regrant requests with the same ID even if retransmitted. Sun currently implements RPC on both TCP/IP and UDP/IP transports. The protocol also supports two special non-RPC uses: batching, where a client sends multiple calls without waiting for replies, and broadcast RPC, where a client broadcasts a request and waits for numerous replies from multiple servers.
sections.eli5: RPC can work over any network protocol. If the network is reliable, you know the function ran. If it is not reliable, you have to guess whether it ran and may need to try again.

sections.title: RPC Message Protocol
sections.content:
Every RPC message begins with a transaction identifier (xid) followed by a union that is either a call message or a reply message, depending on the message type. Call messages contain the RPC version (must be 2 for this specification), the program number, program version, and procedure number. They also include two authentication fields: credentials (identifying the caller to the service) and a verifier (proving the authenticity of the credentials).

Reply messages indicate whether the call was accepted or rejected. If the remote implementation does not support RPC version 2, the reply contains the lowest and highest supported version numbers. If the remote program is unavailable, the procedure number does not exist, or the parameters are invalid, the reply contains an appropriate error code. An accepted reply includes a verifier from the server (allowing the client to authenticate the server) and either the procedure results or error information.

The protocol defines several error conditions: program unavailable, program version not supported (with version ranges returned), procedure unavailable, and garbage arguments. For rejected calls, the server indicates either an RPC version mismatch or an authentication error.
sections.eli5: Each message has an ID number so replies can be matched to requests. Call messages say which program, version, and function to run. Reply messages say whether the call worked or what went wrong.

sections.title: Authentication Protocols
sections.content:
RPC includes several authentication mechanisms. Null authentication is the simplest: the credentials and verifier are empty, used when the caller's identity does not matter or is already known.

UNIX authentication identifies the caller by their user ID, group ID, and group memberships on a UNIX system. The credentials include a machine name, effective user ID, effective group ID, and a list of supplemental group IDs. The server may respond with a shorthand nickname (AUTH_SHORT) that the client can use in subsequent calls instead of transmitting full credentials each time, saving network bandwidth and server CPU cycles. If the server's nickname table is flushed, the client must resend its original credentials.

DES authentication improves on UNIX authentication by using encrypted timestamps to verify that the client possesses the correct encryption key, proving the client's identity. Each client has a network name (netname) instead of a numeric ID, such as unix.515@sun.com, which is unique across the Internet. The client generates a conversation key and sends it encrypted using Diffie-Hellman public-key cryptography with 128-bit keys. The server validates the client by decrypting a timestamp; if the decrypted timestamp is close to the current time, the client must have the correct conversation key. After the first transaction, the server returns a nickname the client can use in further calls. Both client and server must have roughly synchronized clocks for DES authentication to work.
sections.eli5: RPC can identify who is calling in three ways: no check, by UNIX user ID, or by encrypted signature. The encrypted way is safest but requires clocks to be synchronized.

sections.title: Record Marking, Versioning, and Status
sections.content:
When RPC messages are sent over a byte-stream protocol like TCP/IP, the protocol uses record marking to delimit messages. A record is composed of one or more record fragments, each beginning with a four-byte header. The highest-order bit indicates whether this is the last fragment; the remaining 31 bits encode the fragment's length in bytes. All data in RPC messages is encoded using XDR (eXternal Data Representation), a neutral, machine-independent encoding language.

Each RPC program has a version number, allowing a single server to support multiple versions simultaneously for backward compatibility. When a client calls a program that does not support the requested version, the server responds with the lowest and highest supported version numbers. The RPC specification does not define how clients discover which servers host particular programs; this is left to higher-level software.

The RPC protocol itself provides no encryption of data in transit; it only provides authentication and verification fields. Applications requiring confidentiality must implement encryption above the RPC layer, or use a secure transport.

RFC 1050 is a historical specification from Sun Microsystems. It is no longer an Internet standard, having been superseded by RFC 1057, which provides the official standard version of the same protocol with minor revisions.
sections.eli5: When RPC uses TCP, special markers show where messages begin and end. Each program can have multiple versions so old and new clients both work. RPC lets you know who is calling, but does not hide messages; add encryption if you need secrecy. This was Sun's original RPC design and is now historic.
